messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 34
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: School Counselor
- Trauma Type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
- Pcl5: 77

# The Weight of a Moment

Marcus is a 34-year-old school counselor who has spent most of his adult life helping other people find their footing. He is the kind of man who remembers students' birthdays, who keeps a bowl of granola bars in his office for kids who come in hungry, who genuinely believes that most problems can be worked through if someone is willing to sit with you long enough. For the past two years, however, he has struggled to believe any of that applies to him.

Two years ago, on a Saturday afternoon in early October, Marcus was backing his truck out of his driveway. It was a day like any other — his wife had asked him to make a run to the hardware store, the radio was on, the autumn light was flat and grey. His seven-year-old neighbor, a boy named Daniel, had been riding his bike on the sidewalk and, for reasons no one has ever been able to fully explain, darted behind the truck at precisely the wrong moment. Marcus didn't see him. He felt the impact before he understood what it was — a sound he describes as a "soft thud, like hitting a bag of sand" — and that sound has not left him since.

Daniel survived, but he sustained a severe traumatic brain injury that left him with lasting cognitive and motor impairments. Marcus called 911, stayed with the boy until the ambulance arrived, and held Daniel's hand in the driveway while the child was unconscious. He has not been able to drive since.

In the weeks that followed, Marcus moved through his life as though submerged in water. He returned to work because he didn't know what else to do, but sitting across from students in crisis — teenagers describing car accidents, family violence, sudden losses — became almost unbearable. He finds himself flinching at the sound of tires on pavement outside his office window. He has rearranged his desk so he cannot see the school parking lot.

At home, the situation is quieter but no less painful. His wife, Renata, drives him everywhere now, and though she has never once complained, Marcus is consumed by shame about this. He wakes most nights between two and four in the morning, sometimes from a dream in which he is still in the driveway, sometimes from no dream at all — just a sudden, electric wakefulness and the certainty that something is terribly wrong. He lies in the dark and replays the sequence of events in obsessive, granular detail, searching for the moment he could have done something differently, certain that a more careful, more attentive person would have.

During the day, he is hypervigilant in ways that exhaust him. He scans hallways, parking lots, and crosswalks with an intensity that leaves him depleted by midmorning. He has stopped attending his son's soccer games because the sound of children running and shouting on pavement makes his chest tighten until he cannot breathe. He has largely withdrawn from the neighborhood — he and Renata moved briefly considered moving, and he still avoids the section of the driveway where it happened, entering and exiting through the back door instead.

What troubles Marcus most, in the quiet moments he allows himself to reflect, is the disconnect between who he is professionally and who he has become privately. He counsels students every day about self-compassion, about the difference between guilt and responsibility, about the fact that accidents are not the same as intentions. He believes all of it — for them. For himself, he feels only a cold, immovable certainty that he is the man who hurt Daniel, and that no amount of reframing will change what that sound felt like, or what Daniel's face looked like in the driveway, or the fact that a little boy's life was permanently altered in the time it takes to back out of a driveway on an ordinary Saturday afternoon.

He has not spoken about any of this to anyone at work. He is, after all, the one people come to.
